items.prompt: Ben and Rosa have both guessed rain for 20 years. When Rosa says '90% confident,' it rains about 89% of the time. When Ben says '90% confident,' it rains only about 58% of the time. What does this difference actually measure?
choices: Who has read more about weather forecasting
Whether a stated confidence level matches the actual hit rate across many such calls
Who is naturally more optimistic
Who has better eyesight for reading clouds
items.explanation: Calibration measures the match between a stated confidence number and the real hit rate for calls made at that confidence level — not general knowledge, personality, or any one-off guess. Rosa's numbers track reality closely; Ben's don't, even with identical experience.
items.reference:
The claim: Calibration is about whether your stated confidence matches your actual hit rate — not about how many facts you know.

Why: Ben and Rosa both guessed rain for 20 years. Rosa's '90% confident' calls are right ~89% of the time; Ben's are right only ~58% of the time — same experience, different calibration.

items.explanation: Well-calibrated is specifically about the match between a stated confidence level and the actual hit rate at that level, checked across many predictions — not about raw accuracy or caution.
items.reference:

items.prompt: After four months, is Tomás's calibration gap closing the same thing as him simply getting more predictions right overall?
choices: Yes, closing the gap always means a higher raw success rate
Not necessarily — his gap closed mainly because his stated confidence numbers became more honest about his real hit rate, not because that hit rate itself shot up to near-100%
Yes, because well-calibrated always means always correct
No, because calibration and accuracy are entirely unrelated and never interact
items.explanation: Improved calibration is about the stated number matching the real hit rate, whatever that hit rate is. Tomás's '80% confident' calls landing at ~80% actual doesn't require his underlying skill at the tasks to have jumped to near-perfect — it requires his self-assessment to have become more honest.
items.reference:
The claim: Improving calibration means closing the gap between stated confidence and actual hit rate — not necessarily getting more predictions right overall.

Why: Tomás's gap closed by his stated numbers becoming more honest about his existing hit rate, not by his hit rate itself jumping to near-100%.

items.prompt: Could someone become better calibrated while their actual skill at the underlying task stays exactly the same?
choices: No, calibration and skill are the same thing by definition
Yes — calibration is about the accuracy of self-assessed confidence, which can improve independently of whether the underlying skill itself changes
No, calibration can only improve if the person also gets objectively better at the task
Yes, but only in domains that involve weather or debugging specifically
items.explanation: Calibration tracks how well stated confidence matches real hit rate — someone can learn to state more honest confidence numbers about a skill level that isn't itself changing, which is a real and valuable form of improvement on its own.
